pages.title: Al-Andalus and a Great Traveler
pages.content:
Muslims ruled some parts of Spain and Portugal from 711 to 1492. People called this land Al-Andalus. For 781 years of Islamic rule in Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians, and Jews lived side by side, and often worked, traded and studied together. They built one of the greatest cultures of the Middle Ages in the West. They created many special works in art, architecture, medicine, literature, and philosophy. Al-Andalus was in Europe because of its location and its people, but it was a part of the Islamic West, too.

Many famous people lived in Al-Andalus. Ibn al-Arabi was a thinker and poet. Ibn Rushd was a scientist, thinker, and doctor. Ibn Tufayl was a writer and doctor.

After Muslims took control of Spain in the 700s, the connection between Europe and the Middle East became stronger. Christian, Jewish, and Muslim people traveled a lot because they wanted to trade, learn more, and visit holy places. Ibn Jubayr was also one of the most important travelers of the Middle Ages from Al-Andalus.

When Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia in the year 1145, Muslim Spain was rich in culture and learning. Valencia is a famous city in the east of Spain, near the sea. In the tenth century, Granada was bigger than most cities in Western Europe and the east. Sevilla was also a big city with 500 bathhouses and 1,000 mosques. Córdoba had 700,000 people, so it was the largest city in Western Europe. This great culture surprised the people of that time because Muslims lived a much better life than them. Historians say that Islamic Spain brought great culture and knowledge to the rural life of Western Europe.

pages.title: A Young Scholar from Granada
pages.content:
When you think of the great travelers of the Middle Ages, what are the first two names that come to mind? For sure, they are Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta. But in this text, you will learn about another important traveler: Ibn Jubayr.

In the late 12th century (1183–1185), Ibn Jubayr went from Al-Andalus to the Holy Land. He traveled about 15,000 kilometers.

Later, in the late 13th century (1271–1295), Marco Polo traveled about 24,000 kilometers to China. In the 14th century (1325–1354), Ibn Battuta traveled a very long way, about 117,000 kilometers. He went much further than the other two travelers.

Ibn Jubayr traveled less, but he was one of the first great travelers because he wrote one of the first travel books. So, he was an important guide for later travelers like Ibn Battuta.

When he was young, Ibn Jubayr studied hard and learned more about Islam, languages and literature. He had a good education. When he grew up, he got a job with the government and worked as a secretary for the governor of Granada. One of his biggest dreams was to go on Hajj. He also wanted to gain new knowledge and skills during his journey to Mecca. Another goal of this trip was to get information about other Muslim lands. So, he visited great Eastern cities like Baghdad, Mosul, Aleppo, Jerusalem and Damascus.

When he started his long journey in 1183, he was a middle-aged man from a well-known family in Al-Andalus.

pages.title: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
pages.content:
Ibn Jubayr was not the first person from Al-Andalus to travel for Hajj. But he was one of the first to carefully write about his trip and share his stories with many other people. Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey. The name of his travel book is the Rihla. In the Arabic language, the word rihla means travel book. This book made him very famous in history because his diary became the model for a whole new kind of travel book.

Today, everyone knows this book as the Rihla of Ibn Jubayr. Ibn Jubayr wrote down everything he saw and heard almost every day while he still remembered the details. This old travel book opens a magical window into the Mediterranean journeys in the twelfth century. This helps the reader imagine everything Ibn Jubayr saw. He describes both daily life and amazing sights. For example, when you read his travel book, you can see big storms hitting ships. You can also imagine large crowds of pilgrims in Mecca. At that time, Crusaders were in Palestine. Ibn Jubayr wrote about Muslim prisoners. You can also see that Crusaders sold Muslim slaves in the market.

In the Middle Ages, the journey to Mecca for Hajj was very long and difficult. It was much harder than today. At the end of the twelfth century, the Mediterranean Sea and the lands around it were very dangerous. Almost the whole area was a war zone. Christian Crusaders were attacking Muslim lands. So, under these difficult conditions, Ibn Jubayr’s long journey took two years and three and a half months. He traveled by boat, by camel, and on foot to visit Mecca.

pages.title: Across the Mediterranean
pages.content:
On February 3, 1183, Ibn Jubayr left Granada and went to Ceuta. Ceuta was a Muslim city in North Africa. There, he took a Genoese ship and passed the islands of Sardinia and Sicily. When Ibn Jubayr was on a ship near Sardinia, he wrote that he saw 80 Muslim prisoners. The Crusaders were selling them as slaves at the market.

While they were sailing between these islands, a terrible storm caught them. After the storm stopped, the ship continued on its way toward the island of Crete. Then, it turned south towards Egypt and finally arrived in Alexandria on March 26. At that time, traveling by sea was faster and safer than traveling by land. That’s why Ibn Jubayr followed this interesting route.

Ibn Jubayr got off the ship in Alexandria. This time he saw a group of Christian soldiers there. They were prisoners. These Christian soldiers used to attack Muslims on their Hajj journey. But an army from Cairo managed to stop them just one day away from Medina. Ibn Jubayr also saw this and wrote it in his travel book.

In Alexandria, Ibn Jubayr went to see the famous Lighthouse of Alexandria. It was still standing during that time. The very big size and beauty of the lighthouse amazed him. He wrote that it was more than 50 men tall and it was very old and strong. After he stayed there for eight days, he traveled to Cairo.

pages.title: Cairo under Saladin
pages.content:
Three days later, Ibn Jubayr arrived in Cairo. At that time, Cairo was the capital of the Ayyubid state, and its ruler was Saladin al-Ayyubi. Ayyubid state was a Turkish state. It ruled Egypt, the Middle East, Yemen, and North Africa between 1171 and 1462.

Ibn Jubayr felt great respect for Sultan Saladin. He praised Saladin’s kindness and generosity. He wrote: “Sultan Saladin gives support to every single mosque, hospital, and school.” Ibn Jubayr also wrote about Saladin’s fair rules. He did not ask the farmers to pay the Nile water taxes. The roads were also so safe that people could travel day and night without any fear.

He noticed that Saladin was making the city walls longer to protect Cairo from future enemy attacks. He also saw a very large bridge under construction over the Nile River. Workers made it very high to avoid the heavy yearly floods.

Finally, Ibn Jubayr visited a large hospital in Cairo. It was completely free. It had separate areas for men, women, and patients who needed special care. He also saw the famous pyramids and the Sphinx. At the river, he looked at a special tool called a Nilometer. People used it to measure the height of the Nile floods.

In Alexandria and Cairo, Ibn Jubayr saw many colleges and guesthouses. Saladin built these places for students, teachers, and poor people. They could live there, and he also gave them money for their daily needs. The Sultan also built public baths and hospitals, and he sent doctors to take care of sick people at home. Another good thing Saladin did was giving out 2,000 loaves of bread to the poor every day.

pages.title: The Caravan to Mecca
pages.content: Then, he joined a group of travelers in a camel caravan to go to the Red Sea. Ibn Jubayr wrote about the caravans. In the caravans, you could easily see who was rich and who was poor. You only needed to look at their tents. The tents of rich royal people were amazing. They were like beautiful moving palaces.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:ibnjubayr-red-sea
Shelters made of cloth that people sleep in outside.

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: They Were Like …
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 6. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The tents of rich royal people were amazing. They were like beautiful moving palaces.” What does “were like” mean?

pages.title: Eight Months in Mecca
pages.content: At last, he arrived in the Holy City of Mecca in August 1183. He stayed in Mecca for more than eight months and made the Hajj. He describes the Great Mosque of Mecca and the holy Ka’bah with respect. People traveled to Mecca from very far places such as Persia, India, and Africa. In his book he describes Mecca like a poet: “Mecca is located in a narrow valley. However, it can get bigger and have space for a very big crowd of people. This is one of Allah’s amazing miracles. The doctors are right. They say Mecca is like a mother’s body. A mother’s body surprisingly makes enough space for her baby. If you put this same giant crowd into the biggest city on earth, that city cannot hold them.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:ibnjubayr-mecca
Not wide.
Amazing events that show the power of Allah.
Very big.

exercises.title: Like a Mother
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Ibn Jubayr says Mecca is like a mother’s body. Why?
options: Mecca is a very old city.
Mecca is far away from other cities.
Mecca makes enough space for a huge crowd.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 says: “Mecca is located in a narrow valley. However, it can get bigger and have space for a very big crowd of people.” Then: “A mother’s body surprisingly makes enough space for her baby.”

feedback.correct: Yes! The valley is narrow, but it makes space for everyone, like a mother’s body makes space for her baby.
feedback.incorrect: Read Ibn Jubayr’s words about Mecca at the end of Chapter 7. What does a mother’s body do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: Can and Cannot
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read Ibn Jubayr’s words in Chapter 7. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “However, it can get bigger and have space for a very big crowd of people.” and “If you put this same giant crowd into the biggest city on earth, that city cannot hold them.” What do “can” and “cannot” show?
options: what is possible and not possible
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Can + base verb” shows that something is possible: Mecca can have space for the crowd. “Cannot + base verb” shows that it is not possible: the biggest city cannot hold them.

feedback.correct: Correct. Can = possible; cannot = not possible.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences again. Is it about the past, or about what is possible?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: With Respect, Such As
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words tell us how, and which words give examples?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: He describes the Great Mosque of Mecca and the holy Ka’bah [blank] respect. People traveled to Mecca from very far places [blank] Persia, India, and Africa. … A mother’s body [blank] makes enough space for her baby.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “With respect” tells us how he describes the holy places. “Such as” gives examples: Persia, India and Africa are far places. “Surprisingly” is an adverb (surprising + -ly); it comes before the verb makes.

feedback.correct: Well done. With respect = how, such as = examples, -ly before the verb.
feedback.incorrect: Which gap gives examples? Which gap comes before the verb makes?

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: A Special Place
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Describe a special place you know. Say where it is.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you describe a place with “is located in” and “can”?

pages.title: Medina and Baghdad
pages.content: Then, he went to Medina (April 16, 1184) and stayed there for only five nights. From there, he joined a large group of people on a slow journey through the desert. He traveled northeast to Baghdad. He passed near the Euphrates River. At that time, Baghdad was the capital city of the Abbasids. Ibn Jubayr wrote that there were 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques in Baghdad. He describes the city as it was about 75 years before the Mongols attacked in 1258. Then, he went to northern Syria.

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: Words for Moving
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 8 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do to, through, near and for mean in these phrases?

matchingPairs.right: in the direction of a place

matchingPairs.left: a slow journey through the desert

feedback.correct: Correct. You know the small words for moving and time.
feedback.incorrect: Think of a map: Did he go into the river, or close to it? Did he cross the desert?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: Was or Were?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from Chapter 8.
languageFocusExercises.question: When do we use was, were and -ed?

formChoices.sentence: At that time, Baghdad [choice] the capital city of the Abbasids.
Ibn Jubayr wrote that there [choice] 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques in Baghdad.
Then, he went to Medina (April 16, 1184) and [choice] there for only five nights.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: One thing (Baghdad) → was. Many things (2,000 bathhouses) → there were. “Stay” is regular, so the past is “stayed”.

pages.title: Damascus and Its Great Mosque
pages.content:
He went through Aleppo and finally arrived in Damascus. Damascus was the first capital of the old Umayyads. He gives many details about the Great Mosque of Damascus. He describes its size, roof, the dome, the courtyard, and the tall minarets. He also talks about the water basins, the pretty mosaics, the gateways, and the water clock. He describes the prayer places, the special rooms for important people, and the shops next to the mosque. He writes a lot about this famous mosque. He shows us how the mosque looked before Timur burned the city in 1401 and before the great fire of 1893.

In the city of Damascus, Ibn Jubayr also wrote about helpful gifts of money. These gifts helped travelers and students from other countries. They could also stay in madrasas (schools) and not pay for their living costs. These places helped Muslims travel to new places for a short or long time.

__historical_entity__:ibnjubayr-damascus

the workers of the Great Mosque
the shop owners next to the mosque
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9 says: “In the city of Damascus, Ibn Jubayr also wrote about helpful gifts of money. These gifts helped travelers and students from other countries.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 9 again. Find the words “These gifts helped …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: He Describes …
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 9. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He describes its size, roof, the dome, the courtyard, and the tall minarets.” Ibn Jubayr lived long ago. Why does the chapter say “describes”, not “described”?
options: because the visit is happening now
because we are talking about what his book says, and we can still read it
languageFocusExercises.explanation: We often use the present simple to talk about what a book says: “He describes …”, “He also talks about …”. The book is still here, and we can read it today.

feedback.correct: Correct. A book “says” and “describes” in the present.
feedback.incorrect: Think: Can we read his book today? What does the book do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: Help for Students
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form comes after “gifts”, “could” and “not”?

pages.title: Palestine and Acre
pages.content:
From there, he went to Palestine. Palestine was under the control of the Crusaders at that time. Ibn Jubayr stayed in this Christian Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem for about a month. During this time, he spent nearly two weeks waiting at the port city of Acre because he needed good winds to sail.

In 1184, Saladin was attacking the castle of Kerak. The Crusaders built the castle in 1142. In 1187, Saladin turned his eyes to the Crusader lands and attacked Jerusalem. In 1187, Saladin took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders after 88 years. So Ibn Jubayr went to Mecca for the second time to thank Allah.

exercises.title: Two Weeks in Acre
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 10.
exercises.question: Why did Ibn Jubayr wait nearly two weeks in Acre?
options: He was ill and needed a doctor.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each time phrase from Chapter 10 with its meaning.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “About” = more or less. “Nearly” = a little less than. “In” + a year. “After … years” = that many years after another event.

feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 10 again. Which phrase is not exact? Which one is a little less?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: Why and What For?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words say why, and which say what happened?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: … he spent nearly two weeks waiting at the port city of Acre because he needed good winds [blank]. … In 1187, Saladin turned his eyes to the Crusader lands and [blank] Jerusalem. Ibn Jubayr went to Mecca for the second time [blank] Allah …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “To + verb” gives the purpose: good winds to sail, went to Mecca to thank Allah. “Attacked” is the past event.

feedback.correct: Well done. To + verb for a purpose; -ed for a past event.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each gap: Is it a purpose (what for?) or an event?

pages.title: Going Back Home
pages.content: Acre was one of the most important ports in the Christian Kingdom of Jerusalem. This was the main port, so ships sailed to many different places from here. In 1184, he took a ship to travel back home. He started a journey with fifty other Muslims and two thousand Christian pilgrims from Jerusalem. They traveled west. The trip was very dangerous because of big storms. That’s why their ship hit the ground near the coast of Sicily. Ibn Jubayr almost died, but he survived. The Norman king of Sicily, the Christian ruler King William II, helped the passengers. Ibn Jubayr records that William II could read and write Arabic. Then, he waited for better weather to take another ship home from Sicily. In the end, in 1185, he passed Sardinia and reached the coast of Spain. He arrived back home. He wrote that his journey took two years and three and a half months. The journey was dangerous, but he stayed alive. His heart was full of thanks to Allah for keeping him safe and making his dream come true. Throughout his journey, he was always with Allah. When he was in trouble or danger, he always prayed.

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: Almost Died, But …
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 11. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Ibn Jubayr almost died, but he survived.” What happened to him?
options: He was very near to death, but he stayed alive.

feedback.incorrect: Read the part after “but”. Did he die?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: In 1184, Then, In the End
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: A Hard Day with a Happy End
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tell your partner about a hard day that ended well.

pages.title: Dangers of Medieval Travel
pages.content:
Ibn Jubayr had many adventures during his journey. He even faced deadly dangers because travel in the Middle Ages was really dangerous. It did not matter how people traveled. By sea, big storms and shipwrecks were very real dangers. Ibn Jubayr survived both of them. He almost lost his life during these times. By land, groups of desert robbers were a big problem. They attacked the caravans. They took everything from the travelers. Then, the travelers had to walk to find safety or die under the burning sun.

In fact, the weather and nature could also bring real dangers. The caravans usually traveled at night. This way, they avoided the hot afternoon sun. Travelers also needed to fill their water bags all the time. This situation greatly worried Ibn Jubayr, and he always wrote down the locations of fresh water wells.

vocabulary.definition: Exciting and sometimes dangerous experiences.
Met something difficult or dangerous and had to deal with it.
Be important.
Accidents at sea when a ship breaks or sinks.
People who take things from others by force.
Get to a safe place.
Stayed away from something bad.
Make something full.
Deep holes in the ground with clean water that people can drink.

exercises.title: Dangers of the Journey
exercises.instructions: Match each part of the journey with a danger from Chapter 12.
exercises.question: What were the dangers?

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: Had To
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 12. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Then, the travelers had to walk to find safety or die under the burning sun.” What does “had to walk” mean?
options: They wanted to walk for fun.
Walking was necessary; they had no other choice.
They walked in the past every day.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Had to + base verb” is the past of “have to”. It shows that something was necessary: The robbers took everything, so the travelers had no other choice.

feedback.correct: Correct. Had to = it was necessary in the past.
feedback.incorrect: What did the robbers take? Could the travelers choose another way?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: Needed, Avoided, Had To
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from Chapter 12.

This way, they [choice] the hot afternoon sun.

feedback.correct: Correct. Past -ed, and had to + base verb.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word before each gap. After “had to”, does the verb change?

pages.title: Return, Later Life, and Lessons
pages.content:
When Ibn Jubayr returned to Granada, he began writing his travel book and continued his studies. He taught hadiths of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh). (Hadiths are the words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.) After his wife’s death, he started his third long trip to Mecca for the pilgrimage. He stayed in Mecca for some time. Finally, he moved to Alexandria and died there in 1217. Muslim thinkers often traveled to the East for knowledge. Ibn Jubayr was also one of them.

At the start of his journey, Ibn Jubayr felt very excited about his trip. However, he never thought his Hajj would become such a big adventure. He survived a terrible shipwreck and escaped the great dangers of the desert. But outside of these dangers, his journey taught him a lot. His main goal was the Hajj, but he also gained many new experiences. For him, learning was just as important as Hajj. He completed the journey, visited Mecca for Hajj, and met other Muslims from the Islamic world. He could never find these experiences back home in Al-Andalus. In the end, he learned many things that he could not learn at home in Granada. His journey made him a wiser person.

Ibn Jubayr thought that other people should do the same. He told young people to leave their home country and travel to look for knowledge.

vocabulary.definition: What you know and understand after you learn.
Something that you want to do or get.
Having more knowledge and better judgment than before.
Try to find.

exercises.title: Advice for Young People
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 13.
exercises.question: What did Ibn Jubayr tell young people to do?
options: to stay at home and study hard
to travel and look for knowledge
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “He told young people to leave their home country and travel to look for knowledge.”

feedback.correct: Yes! His journey made him wiser, so he thought other people should travel and learn, too.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Find the words “young people”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Look: Should
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 13. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Ibn Jubayr thought that other people should do the same. He told young people to leave their home country and travel to look for knowledge.” What does “should” show?
options: advice: A good idea for other people
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Should + base verb” gives advice: it is a good idea. Ibn Jubayr learned a lot, so he gave this advice to young people. “Told + person + to + verb” reports the advice.

feedback.correct: Correct. Should = advice; told … to … = reported advice.
feedback.incorrect: Is it a law, or a good idea from a wise person?

languageFocusExercises.title: Practise: What He Learned
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Ibn Jubayr learn from his journey?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: For him, learning was just as [blank] as Hajj. … In the end, he learned many things he [blank] learn at home in Granada. His journey made him a [blank] person.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Just as + adjective + as” means the same: Learning and Hajj were equally important. “Could not” = was not possible in the past. “Wiser” compares him before and after the journey.

feedback.correct: Well done. As important as, could not, wiser.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 13 again. After “just as” the adjective does not change.

feedback.correct: Check: should + base verb, and a reason with because or so.

places.name: Valencia
places.text: Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia in 1145. Valencia is a famous city in the east of Spain, near the sea.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 1. At that time Valencia was part of Al-Andalus, the lands in Spain and Portugal that Muslims ruled from 711 to 1492.
places.question: In which year was Ibn Jubayr born?

places.name: Granada
places.text: Ibn Jubayr worked as a secretary for the governor of Granada. On February 3, 1183, he left Granada for his long journey. When he came back, he began writing his travel book here.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 2, 4 and 13. Granada is the start and the end of the journey.
places.question: What was Ibn Jubayr’s job in Granada?

places.name: Ceuta
places.text: Ceuta was a Muslim city in North Africa. Here, Ibn Jubayr took a Genoese ship.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 4. The book does not say how he went from Granada to Ceuta, so this part of the line is only a guide.
places.question: Where did Ibn Jubayr take a ship?

places.name: Sicily
places.text: On the way home, big storms made the ship hit the ground near the coast of Sicily. Ibn Jubayr almost died. The Norman king of Sicily, King William II, helped the passengers.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 4 and 11. On the way to Egypt, a terrible storm caught the ship between Sardinia and Sicily. The book does not name the place of the shipwreck, so the map marks the whole island.
places.question: Who helped the passengers after the shipwreck?

places.name: Alexandria
places.text: The ship arrived in Alexandria on March 26, 1183. Ibn Jubayr saw the famous Lighthouse of Alexandria. It was more than 50 men tall. At the end of his life, he moved to Alexandria and died there in 1217.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 4 and 13. The sea line goes past the islands the book names: Sardinia, Sicily and Crete. The book gives no exact route. Near Sardinia, he saw 80 Muslim prisoners; the Crusaders were selling them as slaves at the market. In Alexandria, he saw Christian soldiers as prisoners; an army from Cairo managed to stop them one day away from Medina.
places.question: What famous building did Ibn Jubayr see in Alexandria?

places.name: Cairo
places.text: Cairo was the capital of the Ayyubid state. Its ruler was Saladin. Ibn Jubayr saw a free hospital, a very large bridge over the Nile, the pyramids and the Sphinx.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 5. He arrived in Cairo three days after he left Alexandria.
places.question: Who was the ruler in Cairo at that time?

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Ibn Jubayr arrived in Mecca in August 1183. He stayed there for more than eight months and made the Hajj. People came to Mecca from Persia, India and Africa.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 6–7. The book says only that he joined a camel caravan to go to the Red Sea. It names no stops, so the line from Cairo is only a guide.
places.question: How long did Ibn Jubayr stay in Mecca?

places.name: Medina
places.text: Ibn Jubayr went to Medina on April 16, 1184. He stayed there for only five nights.
places.question: How many nights did Ibn Jubayr stay in Medina?

places.name: Baghdad
places.text: From Medina, Ibn Jubayr traveled northeast through the desert. He passed near the Euphrates River. Baghdad was the capital city of the Abbasids. It had 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 8. The line through the desert is only a guide. Mosul is named in chapter 2 and is shown as a small town on the way north.
places.question: Which river did Ibn Jubayr pass near on the way to Baghdad?

places.name: Aleppo
places.text: After Baghdad, Ibn Jubayr went to northern Syria. He went through Aleppo on his way to Damascus.
places.question: Which city did Ibn Jubayr go through before Damascus?

places.name: Damascus
places.text: Damascus was the first capital of the old Umayyads. Ibn Jubayr wrote a lot about its Great Mosque: the dome, the courtyard, the mosaics and the tall minarets.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 9. Gifts of money helped travelers and students here. They could stay in madrasas and not pay for their living costs.
places.question: Which famous building in Damascus did Ibn Jubayr describe?

places.name: Acre
places.text: Acre was an important port in the Christian Kingdom of Jerusalem. Ibn Jubayr waited here for nearly two weeks because he needed good winds to sail. In 1184, he took a ship to travel back home.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 10–11. Palestine was under the control of the Crusaders at that time. Kerak, the castle that Saladin was attacking in 1184, is shown as a small town.
places.question: Why did Ibn Jubayr wait in Acre?

places.name: Jerusalem
places.text: At that time, Jerusalem was in the hands of the Crusaders. In 1187, Saladin took Jerusalem back. Ibn Jubayr went to Mecca for the second time to thank Allah.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 2 and 10. Chapter 2 names Jerusalem among the great cities he visited, but the book gives no details of the visit, so no line goes there.
places.question: Who took Jerusalem back in 1187?

exercises.title: Living Together
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: In Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side. What did they often do?
options: They worked, traded and studied together.
They only met at the market once a year.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Muslims, Christians, and Jews lived side by side, and often worked, traded and studied together.”

feedback.correct: Yes! They lived side by side and often worked, traded and studied together. Together they built a great culture.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 1 again. Find the words “side by side”.

exercises.title: Starting the Journey
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: Ibn Jubayr was a very young man when he started his long journey in 1183.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “When he started his long journey in 1183, he was a middle-aged man from a well-known family in Al-Andalus.”

exercises.title: A Famous Book
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Why did the Rihla make Ibn Jubayr very famous in history?
options: It was the first book in the Arabic language.
It became the model for a whole new kind of travel book.
It was a book about the history of Granada.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “This book made him very famous in history because his diary became the model for a whole new kind of travel book.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Later writers followed his example, so his diary became a model.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 3 again. Find the word “because”.

exercises.title: The Lighthouse of Alexandria
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was still standing when Ibn Jubayr visited it.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “In Alexandria, Ibn Jubayr went to see the famous Lighthouse of Alexandria. It was still standing during that time.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. He saw it and wrote that it was more than 50 men tall.
feedback.incorrect: Read the paragraph about the lighthouse in Chapter 4 again. Find the words “still standing”.

exercises.title: A Hospital in Cairo
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: What was special about the large hospital in Cairo?
options: It was only for rich people.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Finally, Ibn Jubayr visited a large hospital in Cairo. It was completely free. It had separate areas for men, women, and patients who needed special care.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Everyone could get help there, and it had separate areas for men, women and patients who needed special care.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the fourth paragraph of Chapter 5 again. Find the word “free”.

exercises.title: Baghdad
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: What was Baghdad at the time of Ibn Jubayr’s visit?
options: the capital city of the Abbasids
the first capital of the Umayyads
a port city of the Crusaders
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “At that time, Baghdad was the capital city of the Abbasids.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Baghdad was the Abbasid capital, with 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read Chapter 8 again. Find the word “capital”.

exercises.title: The Great Mosque of Damascus
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Why is Ibn Jubayr’s writing about the Great Mosque of Damascus so useful today?
options: It tells us who built the mosque.
It shows the mosque before the big fires.
It shows how the mosque looks today.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “He writes a lot about this famous mosque. He shows us how the mosque looked before Timur burned the city in 1401 and before the great fire of 1893.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Fires changed the mosque later, but his book shows how it looked in his time.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 9 again. Find the word “before”.

exercises.title: Learning and Hajj
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: For Ibn Jubayr, learning was just as important as Hajj.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13: “His main goal was the Hajj, but he also gained many new experiences. For him, learning was just as important as Hajj.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. He went for Hajj, but he also learned many things he could not learn at home.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Find the words “just as important”.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the grammar patterns and language functions from all thirteen chapters.

exercises.title: Look: Two Kinds of Past
exercises.instructions: Look at the past verb. Put each sentence in the right group.
exercises.question: Does the verb add -ed, or does it change?

items: He praised Saladin’s kindness and generosity.
Ibn Jubayr visited a large hospital in Cairo.
Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey.
He also saw the famous pyramids and the Sphinx.
Ibn Jubayr felt great respect for Sultan Saladin.

The verb adds -ed: He praised Saladin’s kindness and generosity.
Ibn Jubayr visited a large hospital in Cairo.
The verb changes (no -ed): Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey.
He also saw the famous pyramids and the Sphinx.
Ibn Jubayr felt great respect for Sultan Saladin.

exercises.explanation: The book tells Ibn Jubayr’s journey in the past. Many verbs add -ed: travel → traveled, praise → praised, visit → visited. Some verbs change and do not take -ed: write → wrote, see → saw, feel → felt. Learn these past forms one by one.

feedback.correct: Well done. You found the -ed verbs and the verbs that change.
feedback.incorrect: Say the verb today (travel, write, see …). Does the past form only add -ed, or does it change?

exercises.title: Look: When and How Long?
exercises.instructions: Match each time phrase from the book with its meaning.
exercises.question: What does each time phrase tell us?
exercises.explanation: Use “in” with a year (in 1145) and “on” with a date (on February 3). “For” tells us how long: He stayed in Alexandria for eight days. “Three days later” tells us the time after another event: Three days after he left Alexandria, he arrived in Cairo.

feedback.correct: Correct. In + year, on + date, for + how long, … later + time after.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the small word in each phrase: in, on, for, later. Which one is about a year, a date, how long or after?

exercises.title: Look: Comparing Two Things
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 4: “At that time, traveling by sea was faster and safer than traveling by land.” What does this sentence do?
options: It says that sea and land travel were the same.
It compares two ways of traveling.
It says that land travel was faster.
exercises.explanation: “Faster” and “safer” are comparatives: short adjective + -er (fast → faster, safe → safer). “Than” comes before the second thing: Traveling by sea … than traveling by land. That’s why Ibn Jubayr chose the sea route.

feedback.correct: Correct. Adjective + -er + than compares two things.
feedback.incorrect: Find the word “than” in the sentence. What two things come before and after it?

exercises.title: Practise: Reason, Result, Different Idea
exercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word gives a reason, a result or a different idea?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Christian, Jewish, and Muslim people traveled a lot [blank] they wanted to trade, learn more, and visit holy places. … This was the main port, [blank] ships sailed to many different places from here. … The trip was very dangerous because of big storms. [blank] their ship hit the ground near the coast of Sicily. Ibn Jubayr almost died, [blank] he survived.
exercises.explanation: “Because” + a sentence gives a reason. “So” and “That’s why” give a result: First the reason, then what happens. “But” gives a different idea: He almost died, but he survived. “Because of” needs a noun after it (“because of big storms”), not a sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked reasons, results and different ideas.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next part give a reason, a result, or a different idea? Check Chapter 1 and Chapter 11.

exercises.title: Practise: Bigger, Harder, Most Important
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: Do we compare two things, or one with all the others?

formChoices.sentence: In the tenth century, Granada was [choice] than most cities in Western Europe and the east.
In the Middle Ages, the journey to Mecca for Hajj was very long and difficult. It was much [choice] than today.
Ibn Jubayr was also one of the [choice] travelers of the Middle Ages from Al-Andalus.

exercises.explanation: With “than”, use the comparative: big → bigger (double g), hard → harder. “Much” makes it stronger: much harder. With “one of the …”, use the superlative: The most important. Long adjectives use more / most, not -er / -est.

feedback.correct: Correct. -er / more + than for two things; the -est / the most for the top of a group.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “than” or “one of the” in each sentence. Check Chapters 1 and 3.

exercises.title: Practise: Fix One Mistake
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct word.
exercises.question: Can you fix the past forms?

errorItems.sentence: In 1184, he taked a ship to travel back home.
He also seed the famous pyramids and the Sphinx.
Ibn Jubayr wrote that there was 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques in Baghdad.

exercises.explanation: “Take” and “see” change in the past: took, saw (not taked, seed). With a plural noun (2,000 bathhouses), use “there were”, not “there was”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed all three sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: Chapter 11 (the ship home), Chapter 5 (the pyramids) and Chapter 8 (Baghdad).

exercises.title: Practise: By Boat, By Camel …
exercises.instructions: Put the words in order to make the sentence from Chapter 3.
exercises.question: How do we say how someone travels?
exercises.explanation: Use “by” + a way of traveling with no “a” or “the”: by boat, by camel, by sea, by land. But say “on foot” for walking. “To + verb” gives the purpose: to visit Mecca.

feedback.correct: Well done. By + transport, on foot, and to + verb for the reason.
feedback.incorrect: Start with “He traveled”. Then list the ways of traveling. End with why he traveled.

exercises.title: Use: A School Trip
exercises.instructions: Complete this new text from the word bank. Two words are extra.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words to write about a trip?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last spring, our class [blank] to Konya by bus. The bus was [blank] than the train. We stayed there [blank] two days. On the first day, we [blank] a big museum, and our teacher told us about its history.
exercises.explanation: “Traveled” and “visited” are regular past verbs with -ed. “Cheaper than” compares two things. “For two days” tells us how long. Like Ibn Jubayr’s diary, the text tells a journey in the past.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new place.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each gap: A past verb? a comparison with than? how long?

exercises.title: Use: My Travel Diary
exercises.instructions: Write 4–5 diary sentences about a trip. Tell a partner first.
exercises.question: Can you write about your own trip?
exercises.explanation: Example: “On July 10, I traveled to Antalya by bus with my family. We stayed there for five days. The sea was warmer than the sea in my town. I saw an old castle, and I learned a lot about its history. That’s why I want to go there again.”

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: a date, by + transport, for + how long, a comparison with than, past verbs, a result.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say when and how: “On …, I traveled to … by …”
discussionPrompts.example: On a Saturday in May, I traveled to Konya by train.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say how long: “We stayed there for …”
discussionPrompts.example: We stayed there for two days.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Compare: “… was bigger / older / more beautiful than …”
discussionPrompts.example: The museum was bigger than our school.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what you saw, and a result: “I saw … . That’s why …”
discussionPrompts.example: I saw many old books and pictures. That’s why I want to learn more about history.

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place.

vocabulary.definition: Bought and sold things.
vocabulary.storyExample: For 781 years of Islamic rule in Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians, and Jews lived side by side, and often worked, traded and studied together.

vocabulary.definition: The place where something is.
vocabulary.storyExample: Al-Andalus was in Europe because of its location and its people, but it was a part of the Islamic West, too.

vocabulary.definition: Knowledge that people get by studying.
vocabulary.storyExample: When Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia in the year 1145, Muslim Spain was rich in culture and learning.

vocabulary.definition: Of the countryside, not the city.
vocabulary.storyExample: Historians say that Islamic Spain brought great culture and knowledge to the rural life of Western Europe.

vocabulary.definition: Public buildings where people go to wash.
vocabulary.storyExample: Sevilla was also a big city with 500 bathhouses and 1,000 mosques.

vocabulary.definition: Come into your thoughts quickly.
collocations: the first names that come to mind
vocabulary.storyExample: When you think of the great travelers of the Middle Ages, what are the first two names that come to mind?

vocabulary.definition: A longer way; to a place that is farther away.
vocabulary.storyExample: He went much further than the other two travelers.

vocabulary.definition: Learn new things.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also wanted to gain new knowledge and skills during his journey to Mecca.

vocabulary.definition: A journey to a place.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: But he was one of the first to carefully write about his trip and share his stories with many other people.

vocabulary.definition: A book where a traveler writes what happens on a journey.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey.

vocabulary.definition: Says or writes what something or someone is like.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: He describes both daily life and amazing sights.

vocabulary.definition: Interesting or beautiful things that people go to see.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: He describes both daily life and amazing sights.

vocabulary.definition: Christian soldiers from Europe who fought for the Holy Land in the Middle Ages.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: At that time, Crusaders were in Palestine.

vocabulary.definition: People who are kept in a place and are not free to leave.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr wrote about Muslim prisoners.

vocabulary.definition: People who other people own and who must work without pay.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: You can also see that Crusaders sold Muslim slaves in the market.

vocabulary.definition: An area where there is fighting.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
vocabulary.storyExample: Almost the whole area was a war zone.

vocabulary.definition: Left a ship, bus or train.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr got off the ship in Alexandria.

vocabulary.definition: Was able to do something difficult.
vocabulary.storyExample: But an army from Cairo managed to stop them just one day away from Medina.

vocabulary.definition: Surprised very much.
vocabulary.storyExample: The very big size and beauty of the lighthouse amazed him.

vocabulary.definition: Thought that someone was very good and important.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr felt great respect for Sultan Saladin.

vocabulary.definition: Said good things about someone or something.
vocabulary.storyExample: He praised Saladin’s kindness and generosity.

vocabulary.definition: A building where Muslims pray.
vocabulary.storyExample: He wrote: “Sultan Saladin gives support to every single mosque, hospital, and school.”

vocabulary.definition: Rules that are right and good for everyone.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr also wrote about Saladin’s fair rules.

vocabulary.definition: The feeling you have when you think something bad will happen.
vocabulary.storyExample: The roads were also so safe that people could travel day and night without any fear.

vocabulary.definition: Saw or understood something.
vocabulary.storyExample: He noticed that Saladin was making the city walls longer to protect Cairo from future enemy attacks.

vocabulary.definition: Attacks by people who fight against you.
vocabulary.storyExample: He noticed that Saladin was making the city walls longer to protect Cairo from future enemy attacks.

vocabulary.definition: Being built.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also saw a very large bridge under construction over the Nile River.

vocabulary.definition: A lot of water that covers land that is usually dry.
vocabulary.storyExample: Workers made it very high to avoid the heavy yearly floods.

vocabulary.definition: Not together; apart from each other.
vocabulary.storyExample: It had separate areas for men, women, and patients who needed special care.

vocabulary.definition: Extra help for people who are very sick.
vocabulary.storyExample: It had separate areas for men, women, and patients who needed special care.

vocabulary.definition: Very old, big stone buildings in Egypt with four sides that meet at the top.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also saw the famous pyramids and the Sphinx.

vocabulary.definition: Find the size, height or amount of something.
vocabulary.storyExample: People used it to measure the height of the Nile floods.

vocabulary.definition: Houses where travelers can stay and sleep.
vocabulary.storyExample: In Alexandria and Cairo, Ibn Jubayr saw many colleges and guesthouses.

vocabulary.definition: Buildings where people can go to wash.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Sultan also built public baths and hospitals, and he sent doctors to take care of sick people at home.

vocabulary.definition: Help people who are ill and give them what they need.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Sultan also built public baths and hospitals, and he sent doctors to take care of sick people at home.

vocabulary.definition: Giving things to many people.
vocabulary.storyExample: Another good thing Saladin did was giving out 2,000 loaves of bread to the poor every day.

vocabulary.definition: More than one loaf. A loaf is bread baked in one piece.
vocabulary.storyExample: Another good thing Saladin did was giving out 2,000 loaves of bread to the poor every day.

vocabulary.definition: Shelters made of cloth that people sleep in outside.
vocabulary.storyExample: You only needed to look at their tents.

vocabulary.definition: Here: Very big, beautiful tents that move with the caravan, like palaces.
vocabulary.storyExample: They were like beautiful moving palaces.

vocabulary.definition: Not wide.
vocabulary.storyExample: In his book he describes Mecca like a poet: “Mecca is located in a narrow valley.

vocabulary.definition: Amazing events that show the power of Allah.
vocabulary.storyExample: This is one of Allah’s amazing miracles.

vocabulary.definition: Very big.
vocabulary.storyExample: If you put this same giant crowd into the biggest city on earth, that city cannot hold them.”

vocabulary.definition: A large, dry, hot area with sand and very little water.
vocabulary.storyExample: From there, he joined a large group of people on a slow journey through the desert.

vocabulary.definition: Pictures made with many small pieces of colored stone or glass.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also talks about the water basins, the pretty mosaics, the gateways, and the water clock.

vocabulary.definition: Big doors or openings in a wall where people go in and out.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also talks about the water basins, the pretty mosaics, the gateways, and the water clock.

vocabulary.definition: An old kind of clock that uses water to show the time.
vocabulary.storyExample: He also talks about the water basins, the pretty mosaics, the gateways, and the water clock.

vocabulary.definition: The money you need for food, a home, and other daily needs.
vocabulary.storyExample: They could also stay in madrasas (schools) and not pay for their living costs.

vocabulary.definition: The tall towers of a mosque. The call to prayer is made from them.
vocabulary.storyExample: He describes its size, roof, the dome, the courtyard, and the tall minarets.

vocabulary.definition: The Christian state that the Crusaders made around Jerusalem in the Middle Ages.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr stayed in this Christian Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem for about a month.

vocabulary.definition: Winds that help a ship sail in the right direction.
vocabulary.storyExample: During this time, he spent nearly two weeks waiting at the port city of Acre because he needed good winds to sail.

vocabulary.definition: Travel on water in a ship or a boat.
vocabulary.storyExample: During this time, he spent nearly two weeks waiting at the port city of Acre because he needed good winds to sail.

vocabulary.definition: (Of a ship) touched the land under the water and could not move.
vocabulary.storyExample: That’s why their ship hit the ground near the coast of Sicily.

vocabulary.definition: Stayed alive after a dangerous event.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr almost died, but he survived.

vocabulary.definition: Stayed in a place until something happened.
vocabulary.storyExample: Then, he waited for better weather to take another ship home from Sicily.

vocabulary.definition: Did not die.
vocabulary.storyExample: The journey was dangerous, but he stayed alive.

vocabulary.definition: Happen in real life, after you hoped for it.
vocabulary.storyExample: His heart was full of thanks to Allah for keeping him safe and making his dream come true.

vocabulary.definition: Exciting and sometimes dangerous experiences.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ibn Jubayr had many adventures during his journey.

vocabulary.definition: Met something difficult or dangerous and had to deal with it.
vocabulary.storyExample: He even faced deadly dangers because travel in the Middle Ages was really dangerous.

vocabulary.definition: Be important.
vocabulary.storyExample: It did not matter how people traveled.

vocabulary.definition: Accidents at sea when a ship breaks or sinks.
vocabulary.storyExample: By sea, big storms and shipwrecks were very real dangers.

vocabulary.definition: People who take things from others by force.
vocabulary.storyExample: By land, groups of desert robbers were a big problem.

vocabulary.definition: Get to a safe place.
vocabulary.storyExample: Then, the travelers had to walk to find safety or die under the burning sun.

vocabulary.definition: Stayed away from something bad.
vocabulary.storyExample: This way, they avoided the hot afternoon sun.

vocabulary.definition: Make something full.
vocabulary.storyExample: Travelers also needed to fill their water bags all the time.

vocabulary.definition: Deep holes in the ground with clean water that people can drink.
vocabulary.storyExample: This situation greatly worried Ibn Jubayr, and he always wrote down the locations of fresh water wells.

vocabulary.definition: What you know and understand after you learn.
vocabulary.storyExample: Muslim thinkers often traveled to the East for knowledge.

vocabulary.definition: Something that you want to do or get.
vocabulary.storyExample: His main goal was the Hajj, but he also gained many new experiences.

vocabulary.definition: Having more knowledge and better judgment than before.
vocabulary.storyExample: His journey made him a wiser person.

vocabulary.definition: Try to find.
vocabulary.storyExample: He told young people to leave their home country and travel to look for knowledge.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Show what you understand from the whole story of Ibn Jubayr’s journey.

exercises.title: What Is a Rihla?
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 3 with two words: travel book, holy city, history lesson or long letter.
exercises.question: What does the word rihla mean?
exercises.fillBlanksText: In the Arabic language, the word rihla means [blank].
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3 says: “The name of his travel book is the Rihla. In the Arabic language, the word rihla means travel book.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Ibn Jubayr’s book is a travel book, so its name is the Rihla.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 3. Find the words “the word rihla means”.

exercises.title: A Fair Ruler
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Why did Ibn Jubayr feel great respect for Sultan Saladin?
options: Saladin invited him to his palace.
Saladin gave him a job in Cairo.
Saladin was kind, generous and fair.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 says: “He praised Saladin’s kindness and generosity.” It also says: “Ibn Jubayr also wrote about Saladin’s fair rules.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Saladin supported mosques, hospitals and schools, and his rules were fair.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 5. What did Ibn Jubayr praise?

exercises.title: Traveling in the Heat
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The caravans usually traveled in the hot afternoon.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12 says: “The caravans usually traveled at night. This way, they avoided the hot afternoon sun.”

feedback.correct: Right. They traveled at night to stay away from the burning sun.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 12. When did the caravans usually travel?

exercises.title: Word Meanings
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning in the story.
exercises.question: What does each word mean?

matchingPairs.right: people who travel to a holy place
a group of people and animals that travel together
deep holes in the ground for water

correctAnswer.pilgrims: people who travel to a holy place
correctAnswer.caravan: a group of people and animals that travel together
correctAnswer.wells: deep holes in the ground for water

exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “… imagine large crowds of pilgrims in Mecca.” Chapter 6: “… he joined a group of travelers in a camel caravan …” Chapter 10: “… the port city of Acre …” Chapter 12: “… he always wrote down the locations of fresh water wells.”

feedback.correct: Yes. You found the meaning of each word from its sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Read each word in its sentence in Chapters 3, 6, 10 and 12.

exercises.title: What Did He See?
exercises.instructions: Match each city with something Ibn Jubayr saw or wrote about there.
exercises.question: Which thing goes with each place on Ibn Jubayr’s journey?

matchingPairs.right: a very old and strong lighthouse
a great mosque with a water clock

correctAnswer.Alexandria: a very old and strong lighthouse
correctAnswer.Damascus: a great mosque with a water clock

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: the Lighthouse of Alexandria “was very old and strong”. Chapter 5: “At the river, he looked at a special tool called a Nilometer.” Chapter 8: “Ibn Jubayr wrote that there were 2,000 bathhouses and eleven Friday mosques in Baghdad.” Chapter 9: he talks about “the water clock” of the Great Mosque of Damascus.

feedback.correct: Yes. You remembered the places on his long journey.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 4, 5, 8 and 9.

exercises.title: The Largest City
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one word: largest, smallest, oldest or newest.
exercises.question: What does Chapter 1 say about Córdoba?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Córdoba had 700,000 people, so it was the [blank] city in Western Europe.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “Córdoba had 700,000 people, so it was the largest city in Western Europe.”

feedback.correct: Yes. With 700,000 people, Córdoba was the largest city in Western Europe.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 1. How many people lived in Córdoba?

exercises.title: A Second Journey to Mecca
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Why did Ibn Jubayr go to Mecca for the second time?
options: to look for his old diary
to visit the castle of Kerak
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says: “In 1187, Saladin took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders after 88 years. So Ibn Jubayr went to Mecca for the second time to thank Allah.”

feedback.correct: Yes. He was thankful to Allah when Jerusalem was free again.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 10. Find the words “for the second time”.

exercises.title: The End of His Life
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: At the end of his life, Ibn Jubayr moved to Alexandria and died there.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “Finally, he moved to Alexandria and died there in 1217.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. He moved to Alexandria and died there in 1217.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Find the word “Finally”.

exercises.title: Ibn Jubayr’s Life
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: Can you put the main events of Ibn Jubayr’s life in order?

sequencingItems.text: Ibn Jubayr is born in Valencia.
Ibn Jubayr’s ship hits the ground near Sicily.
Ibn Jubayr leaves Granada for his long journey.

exercises.explanation: He was born in Valencia in 1145 (Chapter 1). He left Granada on February 3, 1183 (Chapter 4). He arrived in Mecca in August 1183 (Chapter 7). On the way home, his ship hit the ground near Sicily (Chapter 11). He died in Alexandria in 1217 (Chapter 13).

feedback.correct: Yes. You followed his whole life, from Valencia to Alexandria.
feedback.incorrect: Use the years in the story: 1145, 1183, 1184 and 1217.

exercises.title: A Christian King
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: What does Ibn Jubayr record about King William II of Sicily?
options: He could read and write Arabic.
He traveled with Ibn Jubayr to Spain.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 says: “The Norman king of Sicily, the Christian ruler King William II, helped the passengers.” and “Ibn Jubayr records that William II could read and write Arabic.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The king helped the passengers, and he could read and write Arabic.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 11. Find the name William II.
